```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
has_vegan   <- requireNamespace("vegan", quietly = TRUE)
has_ggplot2 <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
```

Stage 3 of sheepdog turns the calibrated nightly detection history into
site x month community matrices for multivariate analyses. This vignette
runs that stage on the example data shipped with the package and closes
with an illustrative ordination.

```{r}
library(sheepdog)
```

## The calibrated detection history

The example history is the output of `calibrate()` on simulated BirdNET
predictions for four sites, five species and six months (October 2021 to
March 2022), with five recorded nights per site x month, except for one
recorder failure. In the simulation, occupancy is seasonal (higher in the
rainy months, November to February) and differs among sites and species;
the false-positive scores overlap those of true detections, at rates that
vary among species and sites (`data-raw/make_example_data.R`).

```{r}
ex <- system.file("extdata", "example", package = "sheepdog")
history_file <- file.path(ex, "nightly_detection_history.csv")
history <- readr::read_csv(history_file, show_col_types = FALSE,
                           col_types = readr::cols(night = "c"))
history
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
sites   <- sort(unique(history$site))
species <- sort(unique(history$species))
```

The history covers `r length(sites)` sites (`r sites`) and
`r length(species)` species (`r species`). Each row is a site x species x
night. `n_reliable` counts the detections whose calibrated probability of
being a true positive reached `p_min` in `calibrate()`; `detection_k1` to
`detection_k3` flag nights with at least one, two or three such detections.

## Why the entry rule must be strict

Occupancy models with false positives include an observation layer that
absorbs misidentifications, provided that part of the detections are
confirmed (see `vignette("crywolf-integration")`). Dissimilarity indices and
ordinations have no such layer: a single false positive becomes a species
"present" in a sample and contributes directly to beta diversity.
`community_matrices()` therefore applies three filters.

* **Repetition rule (`k_min`).** A species counts as detected on a night
  only when it had at least `k_min` reliable detections that night (column
  `detection_k<k_min>`). An isolated high-probability detection is more
  likely to be an error than repeated ones.
* **Core species.** Only species whose calibration is reliable at every
  site enter the matrix. If the classifier has lower recall, or a poorer
  calibration, at some sites, the resulting differences in detection would
  appear as artefactual turnover among sites.
* **Minimum effort (`min_nights_month`).** Each cell is the frequency of
  nights with detection, standardised by effort (nights with detection /
  nights recorded at that site x month). Cells with fewer recorded nights
  than `min_nights_month` give unstable frequencies and are dropped.

## Choosing the core species

The choice of core species is made by the user, from the calibration
diagnostics written by `calibrate()` (e.g. `calibration_curves.png`); the
package does not make it automatically. `summarise_history()` gives a
complementary view: the number of nights with a reliable detection per site
and species under each repetition rule (shown below for `k_min = 1`).

```{r}
by_site <- summarise_history(history)
by_site |>
  dplyr::select(site, species, nights_k1) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = site, values_from = nights_k1)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
core <- by_site |>
  dplyr::summarise(all_sites = all(nights_k1 > 0), .by = species) |>
  dplyr::filter(all_sites) |>
  dplyr::pull(species) |>
  sort()
never <- by_site |>
  dplyr::summarise(none = all(nights_k1 == 0), .by = species) |>
  dplyr::filter(none) |>
  dplyr::pull(species) |>
  sort()
partial <- setdiff(species, c(core, never))
```

Species with no reliable detection anywhere (`r never`) are cases in which
calibrated probabilities rarely reach `p_min`, because their false-positive
scores overlap those of true detections; in the simulation every species
has a non-zero probability of occupancy at every site. Species reliably detected at some sites only (`r partial`) are
the case the core rule targets: their absence from a site may reflect the
classifier rather than the community. Here the core species are taken as
those with at least one night with a reliable detection at every site
(`r core`). This is a convenient proxy for the example; with real data the
decision rests on the calibration diagnostics, and a species that is truly
absent from some sites should not be excluded on this criterion alone.

```{r}
core <- by_site |>
  dplyr::summarise(all_sites = all(nights_k1 > 0), .by = species) |>
  dplyr::filter(all_sites) |>
  dplyr::pull(species) |>
  sort()
core
```

## Building the matrices

```{r}
mats <- community_matrices(history, core_species = core, k_min = 2,
                           min_nights_month = 5)
names(mats)
```

The effort table lists the recorded nights per site x month and whether the
cell entered the matrices.

```{r}
mats$effort
mats$effort |> dplyr::filter(!included)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
n_cells    <- nrow(mats$effort)
n_included <- sum(mats$effort$included)
dropped    <- mats$effort |> dplyr::filter(!included)
dropped_txt <- paste0(dropped$site, " in ", dropped$month, " (",
                      dropped$n_nights_recorded, " nights)",
                      collapse = "; ")
```

Of the `r n_cells` site x month cells, `r n_included` entered the matrices.
The cell dropped by `min_nights_month = 5` is `r dropped_txt`, the month of
the simulated recorder failure; it remains listed in the effort table with
`included = FALSE`. Effort is approximated by the number of distinct nights
that appear in the history of the site for any species, which is adequate
when detections are dense, as here.

The count matrix holds the number of nights with detection, and the
frequency matrix divides it by the recorded nights:

```{r}
mats$counts
mats$frequency
```

## Sensitivity to the repetition rule

The repetition rule trades false positives against missed detections. The
mean frequency of each core species across cells shows how the matrix
changes with `k_min`:

```{r}
sens <- lapply(1:3, function(k) {
  community_matrices(history, core, k_min = k)$frequency |>
    dplyr::summarise(dplyr::across(dplyr::all_of(core), mean)) |>
    dplyr::mutate(k_min = k, .before = 1)
}) |>
  dplyr::bind_rows()
sens
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
loss <- round(100 * (1 - unlist(sens[3, core]) / unlist(sens[1, core])))
most  <- names(which.max(loss))
least <- names(which.min(loss))
```

From `k_min = 1` to `3`, the mean frequency of `r least` falls by
`r loss[least]`%, whereas that of `r most` falls by `r loss[most]`%. The
rule therefore acts unevenly among species, and its effect on the
ordination should be reported. `k_min = 2` is the default.

## Writing the matrices to disk

`build_community_matrices()` is the wrapper that reads
`nightly_detection_history.csv`, calls `community_matrices()` and writes
the frequency and count matrices and the effort table as CSV files:

```{r}
out <- file.path(tempdir(), "community_matrices")
mats <- build_community_matrices(history_file, out, core_species = core,
                                 k_min = 2, min_nights_month = 5)
list.files(out)
```

## An illustrative ordination

The example has only `r length(sites)` sites, six months and
`r length(core)` core species, so the ordination below illustrates the
workflow; it does not support inference. With so few species, the
ordination adds little to a plot of the raw frequencies. It uses the
**vegan** package, which is suggested but not required by sheepdog.

The dissimilarity is Bray–Curtis on the frequency matrix, which retains the
quantitative information of the frequencies; Jaccard on incidence would
discard it. [CITAR: properties of Bray–Curtis and Jaccard for frequency
data in community ordination] Samples in which no core species was
detected have undefined Bray–Curtis dissimilarity and must be removed
first.

```{r, eval = has_vegan}
freq <- mats$frequency |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    season = ifelse(substr(month, 6, 7) %in% c("11", "12", "01", "02"),
                    "rainy", "dry"),
    label  = paste(site, month)
  )
Y <- as.matrix(freq[, core])
rownames(Y) <- freq$label
empty <- rowSums(Y) == 0
freq$label[empty] # samples removed
freq_ord <- freq[!empty, ]
Y <- Y[!empty, , drop = FALSE]
d <- vegan::vegdist(Y, method = "bray")
```

```{r, include = FALSE, eval = has_vegan}
n_empty <- sum(empty)
n_kept  <- nrow(Y)
```

`r if (has_vegan) paste0("Samples removed for lacking any core species: ", n_empty, "; samples kept: ", n_kept, ".") else ""`

A principal coordinates analysis (PCoA) on the dissimilarity matrix:

```{r, eval = has_vegan}
pcoa <- vegan::wcmdscale(d, eig = TRUE)
expl <- pcoa$eig[pcoa$eig > 0] / sum(pcoa$eig[pcoa$eig > 0])
round(100 * expl[1:2], 1)
sum(pcoa$eig < 0) # negative eigenvalues
scores_pcoa <- data.frame(freq_ord[, c("site", "month", "season")],
                          PCo1 = pcoa$points[, 1], PCo2 = pcoa$points[, 2])
```

Bray–Curtis is not Euclidean, so some eigenvalues are negative;
`wcmdscale()` returns only the axes with positive eigenvalues, and the
percentages above are relative to their sum.

```{r, eval = has_vegan && has_ggplot2, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.5, fig.alt = "PCoA of the site x month samples, coloured by site, with shape by season."}
ggplot2::ggplot(scores_pcoa,
                ggplot2::aes(PCo1, PCo2, colour = site, shape = season)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = sprintf("PCo1 (%.1f%%)", 100 * expl[1]),
    y = sprintf("PCo2 (%.1f%%)", 100 * expl[2]),
    colour = "Site", shape = "Season"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_bw()
```

Samples with identical frequencies share a single point. Non-metric
multidimensional scaling (NMDS) on the same dissimilarity, with stress
reported:

```{r, eval = has_vegan}
set.seed(2026)
nmds <- vegan::metaMDS(d, k = 2, trymax = 50, trace = FALSE)
nmds$stress
```

```{r, eval = has_vegan && has_ggplot2, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.5, fig.alt = "NMDS of the site x month samples, coloured by site, with shape by season."}
scores_nmds <- data.frame(freq_ord[, c("site", "season")],
                          vegan::scores(nmds))
ggplot2::ggplot(scores_nmds,
                ggplot2::aes(NMDS1, NMDS2, colour = site, shape = season)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
  ggplot2::labs(colour = "Site", shape = "Season",
                caption = sprintf("Stress = %.3f", nmds$stress)) +
  ggplot2::theme_bw()
```

The low stress is expected: `r length(core)` species define a
low-dimensional configuration, and a two-dimensional NMDS reproduces it
almost exactly.

### A note on inference

A PERMANOVA (`vegan::adonis2()`) could test for differences between
seasons, but the example does not support that test. There are only
`r if (has_vegan) n_kept else "a few"` samples from `r length(sites)`
sites, and months within a site are not independent replicates: they share
the site, its species pool and its recorder, and consecutive months are
temporally autocorrelated. Restricting permutations to within sites
(`strata = site`) respects the blocking by site but not the temporal
dependence, and the cell dropped for low effort leaves the blocks
unbalanced. The code is shown for completeness and its p-value should not
be interpreted:

```{r, eval = has_vegan}
set.seed(2026)
vegan::adonis2(d ~ season, data = freq_ord, strata = freq_ord$site,
               permutations = 999)
```

A design that supports inference would need more sites per treatment, or a
model that accounts explicitly for repeated measures within sites.
